query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small, controlled amount of cerium (≈1–3 atomic%) into a near‐equiatomic, multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy catalyst will promote the in situ formation of finely dispersed CeOx clusters at the surface. These clusters will act as oxygen buffering sites that not only lower the activation temperature for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation but also mitigate deactivation through H2O and NO poisoning and inhibit nanoparticle sintering, thereby simultaneously improving low‐temperature activity, poisoning resistance, and long‐term durability without increasing platinum-group-metal content.
generation.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element catalyst alloy (e.g., a Cu–Ni–based system with low loadings of Pt/Pd) synthesized without cerium doping.
generation.intervention: Doping the catalyst precursor with 1–3 atomic% cerium during synthesis so that Ce ions are incorporated into the alloy and, upon appropriate thermal treatment, form finely dispersed CeOx clusters preferentially at surfaces and grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Catalytic testing under simulated automotive exhaust conditions including transient temperature cycles (ranging roughly from 150 °C to 850 °C), exposure to realistic amounts of water vapor (e.g., 10 vol%) and low ppm levels of NO, and extended aging tests on the order of hundreds of operating hours to mimic vehicle lifetime degradation.
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ generated, ultra‐dispersed CeOx clusters within the high-entropy matrix, particularly at the catalyst surface and grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The CeOx clusters will serve as oxygen reservoirs that facilitate oxygen storage/release and promote the formation of active oxygen species at lower temperatures. This oxygen buffering improves oxidation kinetics while also dynamically mitigating the blocking effects of H2O and NO. In addition, their presence at interparticle boundaries is expected to restrain nanoparticle sintering during high‐temperature cycling, thereby maintaining the catalyst’s active surface area.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped catalyst, the Ce-doped catalyst is predicted to reach lower light-off temperatures (e.g., a reduction in T50 by roughly 20–40 °C), display a considerably smaller drop in conversion rates (reductions in activity loss <10% over repeated poisoning cycles), and exhibit less sintering and structural degradation after long-term aging tests.
generation.baseline: The undoped near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element catalyst, which under identical testing shows higher oxidation temperatures, greater susceptibility to deactivation by H2O and NO, and more pronounced sintering/structural collapse during simulated aging.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is intended for catalyst systems with near‐equiatomic, multi‐principal‐element compositions that already aim to minimize platinum-group-metal content; it may not directly apply to catalysts with very high noble metal fractions or to materials with inherently different microstructures (e.g., high-surface-area nanofibers versus bulk particles).
generation.uncertainty: The proposal synthesizes insights from the high entropy‐driven sintering-resistance and water tolerance observed in Pt/HEO systems (PMC12224923) and the catalytic improvements from increased configurational disorder in spinel oxides (PMC12005821). The extension to Ce doping in this specific multi‐element alloy to mediate poisoning and durability simultaneously is novel; quantitative improvements in T50 reduction and long-term stability under automotive transient conditions remain to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element catalysts: one set doped with 1–3 at% cerium and an undoped control. Subject both sets to automotive exhaust simulation that includes transient temperature cycles (150–850 °C), exposure to 10 vol% water vapor and representative NO concentrations, and a prolonged aging protocol (e.g., 500 hours of continuous cycling).
measurements: Light-off temperatures (e.g., T50 and T90 for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation)
Catalytic conversion rates recorded under poisoning conditions (quantifying activity drops in the presence of H2O and NO)
Post-aging particle size distributions and microstructural analysis via TEM/HAADF-STEM
Surface chemical state and CeOx cluster verification via XPS and in situ Raman or FTIR spectroscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cerium-doped catalyst does not show a statistically significant improvement—defined as a reduction in T50 of at least 20 °C, a suppression of activity loss by more than 10% under poisoning conditions, and demonstrably reduced sintering compared to the undoped control—then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractEnhancing the activity and stability of earth‐abundant, heterogeneous catalysts remains a key challenge, requiring new materials design strategies to replace platinum‐group metals. Herein, it is demonstrated that increasing the configurational disorder of spinel metal oxides (M3O4, where M is a combination of Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, and Zn) leads to significant improvements in carbon monoxide (CO) oxidation performance. A substantial 63% decrease in the T10 value (temperature to reach 10% CO oxidation) is observed by systematically increasing the number of first‐row transition metals within the spinel oxide. Long‐term stability studies reveal that the most disordered 7‐metal spinel oxide exhibited superior resistance to catalyst deactivation compared to the 4‐metal variant, showing a decrease in activity of only 4.7% versus 12.2% during 14 h of operation. A solventless thermolysis approach is developed to synthesize a series of medium entropy spinel oxide (MESO) and high entropy spinel oxides (HESOs) from discrete, air‐stable molecular precursors. In this work, porous HEO nanofibers were elegantly produced via electrospinning technology, remarkably promoting the sinter‐resistance and water‐tolerance of supported sub‐2.6 nm Pt nanoparticles. Due to the high‐entropy effect, the surface free energy of the whole catalytic system was substantially reduced, thereby diminishing the thermodynamic driving force for sintering. As a result, 2.6‐nm Pt remained stable in size at 4.2 nm after aging even at 950 °C and maintained a size of 2.9 nm after aging at 850 °C in a humid atmosphere. In situ, HAADF−STEM revealed that the HEO nanofibers kept their nanopore structures up to 1000 °C. Therefore, the sinter‐resistant and water‐tolerant Pt/HEO catalytic system maintained 100% CO conversion for more than 338 h and withstood 35‐cycles reaction without declining even in the presence of vapor. This work reveals new insights into the high entropy‐driven sinter‐resistance of Pt species, offering new perspectives for exploring advanced catalytic systems with boosted durability.

cited_evidence.text: These results underline the exceptional thermal stability of Pt nanoparticles, which is attributed to the high‐entropy effect. As shown in Figure 4g, the Pt/HEO‐850 °C catalyst demonstrated excellent stability during CO oxidation at 210 °C, maintaining consistent activity over 338 h with ignorable decline (Table S3, Supporting Information). The Pt/HEO‐850 °C demonstrates a slight decline (2.4%) in the 30‐h running with a low deactivation rate constant (k d) of 3.2 × 10−3 h−1, compared with recent Pt‐based catalysts (Figure 4h).[  ] This result exceeds the thermal stability conventional catalysts, showcasing its superior sinter‐resistance. To simulate hydrothermal conditions, vapor was introduced during testing, and even after 35 consecutive cycles, ignorable performance declines were observed (Figure 4i). In the 36th cycle, the porous structure remained intact, with the Pt nanoparticle size increasing only by 0.1–2.7 nm (Figures S36 and S37, Supporting Information). The durability of Pt/HEO in moisture‐rich environments, such as automotive exhaust systems, underscores its potential as a highly reliable catalyst for CO oxidation.
